meta.title: Hyperscale Ledger — audited NVIDIA datacenter GPU corpus
meta.convention: perf_dense and perf_sparse are separate objects. Where NVIDIA prints only a with-sparsity figure and states the halving rule without printing the dense number, dense is computed and flagged in notes. Where NVIDIA states the rule but the value is genuinely absent, dense is null rather than computed.

tags.F: vendor-published (nvidia.com or an NVIDIA-authored datasheet; mirrors flagged)
tags.null: not published — left empty on purpose

parts.name: Tesla P100 SXM2
parts.notes: NVIDIA datasheet 'Tesla P100 | Oct16'. P100 has NO tensor cores — the 21.2 TFLOPS FP16 is vector (CUDA-core) FP16, not tensor throughput, and is therefore not comparable to later generations' tensor figures. Excluded from the fitted trend for that reason. Transistors/process from NVIDIA's Volta whitepaper GP100 comparison table.

parts.name: Tesla P100 PCIe
parts.interconnect: PCIe Gen3 (no NVLink on this form factor)
parts.notes: A 12GB / 549 GB/s SKU of the same card also existed per the same datasheet line. No NVLink row at all on the PCIe datasheet — only PCIe Gen3.

parts.name: Tesla V100 SXM2
parts.notes: The 125 TFLOPS 'Tensor Performance' figure is tensor-core FP16 with FP32 accumulate — the first generation directly comparable to later dense tensor figures. 16 GB is the 2017 launch config; a 32 GB variant followed in 2018 at the same 900 GB/s. Transistors/process from NVIDIA's Volta whitepaper.

parts.name: Tesla V100 PCIe
parts.notes: Same GV100 die as SXM2, lower clocked and lower power: 112 vs 125 TFLOPS tensor FP16, 250 vs 300 W. A clean illustration of why variant substitution fabricates trends.

parts.name: A100 80GB SXM
parts.tdp_note: 400W standard; HGX A100-80GB custom thermal solution SKU up to 500W
parts.nvidia_headline_convention: prints BOTH figures as 'X | Y*' — dense unmarked, sparse asterisked
parts.notes: Dense values are PRINTED by NVIDIA here, not computed — the A100 page shows 'X TFLOPS | Y TFLOPS*' pairs. This differs from the H100 page, which prints the sparse figure only. Ampere has no FP8 tensor core. Transistors/process from NVIDIA's Ampere architecture blog (not on the spec page).

parts.name: A100 80GB PCIe
parts.interconnect: NVLink Bridge for 2 GPUs 600 GB/s; PCIe Gen4 64 GB/s
parts.notes: NVIDIA publishes IDENTICAL compute figures for 80GB PCIe and 80GB SXM — only memory bandwidth, TDP, form factor and interconnect differ. So on A100 the variant trap is a POWER and BANDWIDTH trap, not a throughput one.

parts.name: A100 40GB PCIe
parts.tdp_note: 'operates unconstrained up to its thermal design power (TDP) level of 250 W'; 'Total board power 250 W'
parts.interconnect: NVLink Bridge for 2 GPUs 600 GB/s; PCIe Gen4 64 GB/s
parts.source_doc: NVIDIA A100 40GB PCIe GPU Accelerator Product Brief, PB-10137-001_v03, September 2020
parts.notes: THE PART BEHIND THE BOOK'S FIGURE. This is the September 2020 launch SKU, at 250 W — matching exactly the 'A100 250 W' rung in Ch. 19 of The Thinking Machine. The 80GB refresh followed in November 2020 at 300 W (PCIe) and 400 W (SXM). So Witt's number is a real, vendor-published A100 TDP; the defect is that it is a 40GB PCIe figure sitting in a series whose later rungs are flagship parts.

parts.name: H100 SXM
parts.nvidia_headline_convention: prints ONLY the with-sparsity figure, asterisked — no dense column
parts.notes: Dense values COMPUTED as exactly half the printed sparse figure, per NVIDIA's own stated convention — they are not printed anywhere on the page. Note the trap: sparse TF32 (989) and dense BF16 (989.5) are the same number to three significant figures, so 'the H100 does 989 teraflops' is ambiguous without further qualification. Transistors/process from NVIDIA's Hopper architecture blog.

parts.name: H100 NVL
parts.nvidia_headline_convention: prints ONLY the with-sparsity figure, asterisked
parts.notes: THE VARIANT TRAP, CONCRETELY: 350–400 W against the SXM part's 700 W, on the same generation and the same GH100 die. Substituting this TDP into a flagship series understates the generation by roughly half. Per-GPU figures as printed; NVIDIA sells H100 NVL as a matched NVLink-bridged pair.

parts.name: H200 SXM
parts.notes: IDENTICAL COMPUTE TO H100. Every tensor and vector figure matches H100 SXM exactly — same GH100 die. The entire H200 uplift is memory: 80→141 GB and 3.35→4.8 TB/s. Counting H200 as a compute generation implies throughput progress that did not occur; the trend line is deliberately flat 2022→2023 for this reason.

parts.name: H200 NVL
parts.interconnect: 2- or 4-way NVLink bridge 900 GB/s per GPU; PCIe Gen5 128 GB/s
parts.notes: Same memory as H200 SXM (141 GB / 4.8 TB/s); differs in TDP (600 W), form factor and interconnect topology.

parts.name: B200
parts.tdp_note: Configurable up to 1,000W in HGX B200 (air-cooled). The same Blackwell die is configurable up to 1,200W in the liquid-cooled GB200 NVL72 platform — two platforms, not a conflict.
parts.interconnect: NVLink 5th gen 1.8 TB/s per GPU; PCIe Gen5 128 GB/s
parts.sparsity_footnote: Preliminary specifications, subject to change. All Tensor Core numbers except FP64 with sparsity.
parts.notes: MIRROR SOURCE, FLAGGED: this is an NVIDIA-authored document ('NVIDIA Blackwell | Datasheet', doc 3384703.Dec24, © 2024 NVIDIA) verified by direct PDF text extraction, but retrieved from a third-party host because NVIDIA's own download pages are login-gated. Figures converted from the source's PFLOPS to TFLOPS for unit consistency. FP8 and FP6 share one published row. 208B transistors is the full dual-die package, not a single reticle-limited die.

parts.name: GB200 NVL72

rack_power_kw_reported.label: The Register — nominal spec, NOT an NVIDIA figure
Vertiv reference architecture, co-developed with NVIDIA — 'up to 132kW per rack'

parts.interconnect: NVLink 5th gen / NVLink Switch System — 130 TB/s aggregate rack-wide
parts.sparsity_footnote: 1. Specification in sparse | dense. 2. Specification in sparse. Dense is one-half sparse spec shown.
parts.nvidia_headline_convention: NVFP4 given as an explicit pair '1,440 | 720 PFLOPS'. FP8/FP6, INT8, FP16/BF16 and TF32 show ONE number each (sparse) with the halving rule stated in a footnote — the dense values are never printed. Recorded as null rather than computed.
parts.notes: NVIDIA PUBLISHES NO RACK POWER FIGURE — neither on the product page nor in the official Blackwell datasheet PDF (both checked directly). The ~120 kW / 132 kW figures in universal circulation are third-party. Rack-level figures independently confirmed against the NVIDIA datasheet's per-GPU table (FP32 80 TFLOPS × 72 = 5,760 exactly; FP64 40 × 72 = 2,880 exactly; INT8 10 POPS × 72 = 720 exactly). Minor inconsistency inside NVIDIA's own collateral: the datasheet cover says 'up to 13.5 TB of HBM3E' while its own spec table and the live page say 13.4 TB.

parts.name: GB300 NVL72
parts.cpu_detail: 2,592 Arm Neoverse V2 cores (rack total) — unchanged from GB200 NVL72

rack_power_kw_reported.label: Lenovo Press — '135 kW TDP per rack', NOT an NVIDIA figure
Lenovo Press — 'up to 155 kW peak depending on workload'

parts.interconnect: NVLink 5th gen — 130 TB/s rack-wide, unchanged from GB200 NVL72
parts.sparsity_footnote: Product page: '1. All Tensor Core specifications are with sparsity unless otherwise noted. 2. Without sparsity.' — but NVIDIA's own Blackwell Ultra datasheet PDF words the SAME rule differently: '1. Specification in Sparse | Dense. 2. Specification in sparse. Dense is 1/2 sparse spec shown.'
parts.nvidia_headline_convention: FP4 shown as '1440 | 1080 PFLOPS' with 1080 marked 'without sparsity'. Other tensor rows show one unmarked (sparse) number with no dense figure printed.
parts.notes: TWO VERIFIED REGRESSIONS. Rack INT8 falls from 720 POPS (GB200) to 24 POPS — confirmed via the Blackwell Ultra datasheet's per-GPU figure of 330 TOPS (330 × 72 = 23.76 POPS ≈ 24). Rack FP64 falls from 2,880 TFLOPS to ~100 TFLOPS (per-GPU 40 → 1.3 TFLOPS). Both roughly 30× cuts, reflecting die area reallocated toward FP4/FP6 and attention acceleration. A newer generation is NOT uniformly faster — it is faster at the precisions it was optimised for and dramatically slower at others. Per-GPU TDP configurable up to 1,400 W (vs 1,200 W for Blackwell); NVIDIA publishes no rack kW.

parts.name: Vera Rubin NVL72
parts.cpu_detail: 3,168 custom NVIDIA Olympus cores (rack total) — a change from Grace's off-the-shelf Arm Neoverse V2

rack_power_kw_reported.label: Hashrate Index — '~190 kW (Max Q)', third-party estimate on a preliminary spec
Hashrate Index — '~230 kW (Max P)', third-party estimate

parts.cpu_memory: 54 TB LPDDR5X (rack total); no bandwidth figure published
parts.interconnect: NVLink 6th gen — 260 TB/s rack-wide; NVLink-C2C 65 TB/s
parts.sparsity_footnote: 1. Preliminary information. All values are up to and subject to change. 2. Dense specification. 3. Peak performance using Tensor Core-based emulation algorithms.
parts.nvidia_headline_convention: A THIRD convention: NVFP4 splits into separate 'Inference' (3,600) and 'Training' (2,520, marked dense) rows rather than sparse|dense. Other precisions publish a 'Training' (dense) row only, with no sparse counterpart at all.
parts.notes: NVIDIA's own product page names this 'Vera Rubin NVL72', not the widely-used media 'NVL144' (which counts the 144 individual dies — each Rubin package integrates two). Every figure carries NVIDIA's own footnote 1: 'Preliminary information... subject to change'. NOT PUBLISHED, left null: rack power, transistor count, process node — third-party sources report ~336B on TSMC N3, but that appears on no NVIDIA page we fetched, so it is excluded. TRAP: the page's FP32 SGEMM (28,800 TFLOPS) and FP64 DGEMM (14,400 TFLOPS) figures are Tensor-Core EMULATED, not native; native FP32 is 9,360 and FP64 is 2,400 TFLOPS. Comparing the emulated figures against earlier generations' native FP64 would overstate by ~6×.

gb200_nvl72_mlperf_v5_0.quote: GB200 NVL72 achieves up to 1,960 TFLOPS of training throughput with Llama 3.1 405B Pretraining benchmark
gb200_nvl72_mlperf_v5_0.precision_reasoning: NVIDIA does not state the number format. It cannot be NVFP4: NVIDIA's own MLPerf Training v5.1 material describes that round as the first-ever NVFP4 training submission, so no v5.0 result is FP4. It is implausibly high for BF16: per-GPU dense BF16 is 2,500 TFLOPS, which would imply 78% model-FLOPs utilisation on a 405B pretrain. Against per-GPU dense FP8 of 5,000 TFLOPS it implies 39% MFU, which is an ordinary figure for a well-optimised run. The comparison basis used on this site is therefore dense FP8, not FP4.
gb200_nvl72_mlperf_v5_0.scale_note: The submission behind this figure ran at roughly 2,500 GPUs. It is evidence about delivered per-GPU throughput at that scale, not about fabric behaviour at 150,000 GPUs.

failure_modes.name: The sparsity asterisk goes missing
failure_modes.what: NVIDIA's headline tensor-core figures are footnoted 'with sparsity' and are exactly twice the dense value. Strip the asterisk and throughput doubles.
failure_modes.example: H100 SXM is quoted at 1,979 TFLOPS BF16. Dense is 989.5. Worse: the H100 page prints only the sparse number, so the dense figure appears nowhere on it — you have to know the rule and halve it yourself.

failure_modes.name: The convention changes between generations
failure_modes.what: The safety rail moved. A100 printed both dense and sparse; H100 prints sparse only; GB200 prints a pair for one precision and a footnoted rule for the rest; Vera Rubin abandons sparse|dense entirely for Inference/Training rows.
failure_modes.example: Four NVIDIA generations, four presentation conventions. For GB300, NVIDIA's product page and its own datasheet PDF state the same rule in different words.

failure_modes.name: Variant substitution
failure_modes.what: SXM and PCIe parts of one generation differ in TDP, bandwidth and sometimes clocks. Mixing them across a series fabricates a trend that no product line actually followed.
failure_modes.example: H100 SXM is up to 700 W; H100 NVL is 350–400 W. Same generation, same die, half the power. Substituting the PCIe figure into a flagship ladder understates the generation by roughly half.

failure_modes.name: Denominator splicing
failure_modes.what: A share-of-total computed on one basis gets attached to a number computed on another. The sentence reads fluently and is arithmetically self-refuting.
failure_modes.example: A widely syndicated summary: a 1 GW facility has '$38 B upfront capex, of which $5 B (60%) is servers and GPUs.' $5 B is 13% of $38 B. The 60% is the annualized-TCO share, fused onto the upfront-capex figure.

corrections.source: The Thinking Machine · Stephen Witt · Ch. 19 'Power'
corrections.title: The book's GPU power ladder mixes product lines
corrections.claim: Chapter 19 presents the escalation of AI power draw as a single series: A100 250 W → H100 350 W → B100 700 W → B200 1,000 W. The chapter's argument is that per-chip power is exploding.
corrections.evidence: Every one of these is a real, vendor-published TDP — but not of the same class of part. 250 W is the A100 40GB PCIe launch SKU; 350 W is the bottom of the H100 NVL/PCIe range. The flagship SXM parts of those generations are 400 W and up to 700 W. B100 and B200 are quoted correctly. So the first two rungs are PCIe-class parts and the last two are flagship parts, in one series.

rows: the A100 40GB PCIe launch SKU — 250 W, vendor-published F
the H100 NVL / PCIe variant (350–400 W configurable)
correct (HGX air-cooled; 1,200 W liquid in GB200 NVL72)

corrections.impact: Compared like-for-like, the flagship SXM ladder is 400 → 700 → 1,000 W — a 2.5× rise across two generations, not the 4× the table implies. This is not a case of wrong numbers; it is inconsistent variant selection, which is a subtler and more common failure. The direction of Witt's argument survives and per-chip power really is climbing steeply; its slope does not survive. That it happens in the chapter specifically about power is the point — these figures are hard to handle even for a careful reporter with direct access to the company.

corrections.title: “Each generation is faster than the last”
corrections.claim: Successive GPU generations are treated as uniformly faster, so a later part can be substituted for an earlier one in any performance comparison.
corrections.evidence: Blackwell Ultra (GB300 NVL72) is roughly 30× slower than Blackwell (GB200 NVL72) at INT8 — 24 POPS per rack against 720 — and roughly 30× slower at FP64, per-GPU 1.3 TFLOPS against 40. Both confirmed against NVIDIA's own Blackwell Ultra datasheet. Die area was reallocated toward FP4/FP6 and attention acceleration.
corrections.impact: “GPU performance” is not one number and it is not monotonic. A newer part is faster at the precisions it was optimised for and can be dramatically slower at others. Any single-number performance trend implicitly picks a precision — and which one it picks determines the answer.

corrections.title: “The GB200 NVL72 rack draws 120 kW”
corrections.claim: A specific rack power figure — usually 120 kW, sometimes 132 kW — is quoted as though it were an NVIDIA specification.
corrections.evidence: NVIDIA publishes no rack power figure at all for GB200 NVL72, on either the product page or the official Blackwell datasheet PDF. Both were checked directly. The 120 kW figure traces to trade press; 132 kW to a Vertiv reference architecture co-developed with NVIDIA. Neither is an NVIDIA-published number. The same is true of GB300 (135–155 kW, Lenovo) and Vera Rubin (190–230 kW, third-party estimate on a spec NVIDIA itself labels preliminary).
corrections.impact: The single most load-bearing input in any data-center capacity model — how much power a rack draws — is not vendor-published. Every downstream figure inherits that. It should be tagged R, carried as a range, and treated as the first thing to ask an operator about.
